meta.title: Advanced English Grammar Test (C1-C2)
meta.description: A comprehensive 30-question test covering advanced English grammar topics at the C1-C2 level.
meta.info: This test includes multiple choice and correction questions focusing on inversion, mixed conditionals, cleft sentences, advanced passive structures, subjunctive mood, participle clauses, and more. All questions are designed to be free from errors and ambiguity, reflecting real C1-C2 English proficiency exam standards.
meta.author: Qwen3.7

data.hint: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence.
data.question: ___ had the committee assessed the full extent of the damage than they authorized the emergency funds.

explanation.text: 'No sooner' is paired with 'than' to indicate that one event happened immediately after another. 'Scarcely' and 'Hardly' are paired with 'when'.
explanation.formula: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + subject + past simple
examples: No sooner had I arrived than the phone rang.
Scarcely had she finished speaking when the audience applauded.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms to complete the mixed conditional sentence.
data.question: If she ___ more attention to the details during the planning phase, we ___ in this financial predicament right now.

C.text: had paid / would not have been

D.text: were to pay / would not be

explanation.text: This is a mixed conditional. The 'if' clause refers to a past unreal condition (past perfect: 'had paid'), while the main clause refers to a present unreal result (would + base verb: 'would not be').
explanation.concept: Combining past unreal conditions with present unreal results
explanation.formula: If + subject + past perfect, subject + would + base verb
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have a better job now.
If she had taken the map, we wouldn't be lost.

data.hint: Choose the correct word to form a cleft sentence for emphasis.
data.question: ___ was the CEO's sudden resignation that sent shockwaves through the entire industry.

explanation.text: An 'it-cleft' sentence is used to emphasize a specific part of the sentence. The structure is 'It + be + emphasized element + that/who clause'.
explanation.formula: It + be (is/was) + emphasized noun phrase + that/who + rest of sentence
examples: It was John who broke the window.
It is the environment that we must protect.

data.hint: Choose the correct advanced passive structure.
data.question: The ancient manuscript is believed ___ in a private collection for over a century before it was recently discovered.

explanation.text: When the action in the infinitive happened before the main verb, we use the perfect infinitive. Since the manuscript received the action, the perfect passive infinitive ('to have been hidden') is required.
explanation.formula: Subject + passive reporting verb + to have been + past participle
examples: The treasure is thought to have been buried here.
He is known to have worked at the company for decades.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.

explanation.text: The mandative subjunctive requires the base form of the verb ('be') after expressions of necessity like 'It is essential that', regardless of the subject.
explanation.formula: It is essential/important/vital that + subject + base verb
examples: It is crucial that he be present at the meeting.
The rules demand that every participant submit their form on time.

data.hint: Choose the correct participle clause to complete the sentence.
data.question: ___ the rigorous training program, the athletes were fully prepared for the upcoming championship.

explanation.text: The perfect participle ('Having + past participle') is used to show that one action was completed before another action began.
explanation.formula: Having + past participle, + main clause
examples: Having finished her homework, she went out to play.
Having lived in Paris for years, he spoke French fluently.

data.hint: Choose the correct modal verb phrase.
data.question: You ___ the report yesterday; the deadline has been extended until next Friday.

explanation.text: 'Needn't have + past participle' is used to express that someone did something in the past that was not necessary.
explanation.concept: Modal Perfect for unnecessary past actions
explanation.formula: Subject + needn't have + past participle
examples: You needn't have brought an umbrella; it didn't rain.
She needn't have worried about the exam; she passed easily.

data.hint: Choose the correct future tense to emphasize duration up to a future point.
data.question: By the end of this month, Dr. Aris ___ on this groundbreaking research continuously for over a decade.

explanation.text: The future perfect continuous ('will have been + verb-ing') is used to emphasize the duration of an action that will be in progress up to a specific point in the future.
explanation.concept: Emphasizing duration up to a future time
explanation.formula: Subject + will have been + verb-ing + for/since + time period
examples: By next year, I will have been living here for ten years.
She will have been teaching for two decades by the time she retires.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative clause structure with a quantifier.
data.question: The conference attracted over five hundred delegates, ___ were first-time attendees.

explanation.text: When a quantifier is used in a non-defining relative clause referring to people, 'whom' must be used after the preposition ('of whom'). 'Many of them' would create a comma splice without a conjunction.
explanation.formula: Quantifier + of + whom/which + verb
examples: I have three brothers, all of whom are doctors.
She wrote several books, none of which became bestsellers.

data.hint: Choose the correct discourse marker for concession.
data.question: ___ the undeniable benefits of the new policy, a significant portion of the workforce remains skeptical about its long-term viability.

explanation.text: 'Despite' is a preposition and must be followed by a noun phrase ('the undeniable benefits'). 'Although' and 'Even though' are conjunctions and must be followed by a clause (subject + verb).
explanation.formula: Despite + noun phrase, + main clause
examples: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
Although it was raining, we went for a walk.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.

multiErrorSegments.text: as much as he should to.
correctAnswers: as much as he ought to.

explanation.text: In elliptical constructions with modal verbs like 'should' or 'ought to', the infinitive marker 'to' is omitted when the main verb is understood from context.
explanation.formula: as + much/little + as + subject + modal verb (without 'to')
examples: You should study as much as you can.
He doesn't exercise as often as he should.

data.hint: Choose the correct phrasal verb to complete the sentence.
data.question: The negotiations ___ when the two parties failed to reach a compromise on the primary issue.

explanation.text: 'Break down' means to fail or collapse, especially in the context of negotiations, discussions, or relationships. 'Break out' means to start suddenly (e.g., a fire or war). 'Break up' means to end a relationship or disperse. 'Break in' means to enter forcibly or interrupt.
explanation.formula: Negotiations/relations + break down
examples: The peace talks broke down after three days.
Their marriage broke up last year.

data.hint: Choose the correct pronoun for extraposition.
data.question: ___ remains to be seen whether the new legislation will have the intended effect on the economy.

explanation.text: 'It' is used as a dummy subject (extraposition) to anticipate the true subject, which is the noun clause 'whether the new legislation will have the intended effect on the economy'.
explanation.formula: It + verb + to-infinitive / that-clause / whether-clause
examples: It remains to be seen if they will arrive on time.
It is obvious that she is the best candidate.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form(s) to complete the sentence. (There may be more than one correct answer).
data.question: I distinctly remember ___ the door before we left, so I am certain it was locked.

explanation.text: The verb 'remember' takes a gerund ('locking') or a perfect gerund ('having locked') when referring to a memory of a completed past action. 'Remember to lock' would mean remembering to perform the action in the future or at that moment, not recalling having done it.
explanation.formula: remember + verb-ing / having + past participle
examples: I remember meeting him years ago.
She remembers having seen that movie before.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.

explanation.text: 'Humanity' is an uncountable abstract noun used in a general sense, so it takes the zero article. 'The' is only used when referring to a specific aspect of humanity (e.g., 'the humanity of the soldiers').
explanation.concept: Zero article with abstract uncountable nouns
explanation.formula: Zero article + abstract noun (general sense)
examples: Nature is beautiful.
Society has changed dramatically.

data.hint: Choose the correct quantifier for the uncountable noun.
data.question: There is ___ evidence to suggest that the ancient civilization had advanced knowledge of astronomy.

explanation.text: 'Evidence' is an uncountable noun. 'A great deal of' is used with uncountable nouns, while 'a few', 'many', and 'a number of' are used with countable plural nouns.
explanation.formula: a great deal of / a large amount of + uncountable noun
examples: There is a great deal of truth in his statement.
She has a large amount of experience in this field.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form based on subject-verb agreement rules.
data.question: Neither the CEO nor the board members ___ aware of the impending merger before the announcement.

explanation.text: With 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the rule of proximity). Since 'board members' is plural, the plural verb 'were' is required.
explanation.formula: Neither + singular noun + nor + plural noun + plural verb
examples: Neither the teacher nor the students were happy.
Neither the players nor the coach is to blame.

data.hint: Choose the correct double comparative structure.
data.question: ___ the company invests in employee training, ___ the overall productivity becomes.

explanation.text: The double comparative structure ('The + comparative ..., the + comparative ...') is used to show that two things change together.
explanation.formula: The + comparative adjective/adverb + clause, the + comparative adjective/adverb + clause
examples: The harder you work, the luckier you get.
The more I learn, the less I know.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form to express regret about the past.
data.question: If only I ___ about the traffic congestion; I would have taken an alternative route.

explanation.text: 'If only' followed by the past perfect ('had known') is used to express regret or a wish about a situation in the past that cannot be changed.
explanation.concept: Past regret with 'If only' + past perfect
explanation.formula: If only + subject + past perfect
examples: If only I had studied harder for the exam.
I wish I had listened to your advice.

data.hint: Choose the correct formal concession phrase.
data.question: ___ I admire her dedication to the project, I cannot endorse her methods.

explanation.text: 'Much as' is a formal, fixed phrase used to introduce a concessive clause, meaning 'although' or 'even though'. 'As much' is not used this way, and 'However' would require an adjective/adverb (e.g., 'However much I admire').
explanation.formula: Much as + subject + verb, + main clause
examples: Much as I like you, I cannot agree with you on this.
Much as he wanted to help, he was unable to do so.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.

explanation.text: This is a third conditional sentence with inversion (omitting 'if'). The 'if' clause uses past perfect ('Had the team realized'), so the main clause must use 'would have + past participle' to describe an unreal past result.
explanation.formula: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle
examples: Had I known, I would have helped.
Should you need any assistance, please let me know.

data.hint: Choose the correct word to form a wh-cleft (pseudo-cleft) sentence.
data.question: ___ I find most troubling about his argument is the complete lack of empirical evidence.

explanation.text: A wh-cleft (or pseudo-cleft) sentence begins with a 'wh-' clause (usually 'What') to emphasize the information that follows the verb 'be'.
explanation.formula: What + subject + verb + is/was + emphasized element
examples: What I need is a good night's sleep.
What she said was completely unexpected.

data.hint: Choose the correct impersonal passive structure.
data.question: ___ that the new software update will resolve the majority of the reported bugs.

explanation.text: The impersonal passive structure uses 'It + passive reporting verb + that-clause' to express general beliefs or expectations without specifying who holds them.
explanation.formula: It + is/was + past participle (of reporting verb) + that-clause
examples: It is expected that the economy will recover.
It was reported that the suspect had fled.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form to fix the dangling modifier.

explanation.text: The participle phrase 'Walking down the street' must logically modify the subject of the main clause. Trees cannot walk, so the subject must be changed to a person (e.g., 'I', 'we', 'she').
explanation.formula: Participle phrase, + subject (that performs the action) + verb
examples: Driving down the road, I saw a deer.
Having finished the meal, the guests thanked the chef.

data.hint: Choose the correct modal verb for logical deduction about the past.
data.question: The lights are off and the car is gone; they ___ left for the weekend already.

explanation.text: 'Must have + past participle' is used to express a strong logical deduction or certainty about a past event based on present evidence.
explanation.formula: Subject + must have + past participle
examples: The ground is wet; it must have rained last night.
She isn't answering her phone; she must have fallen asleep.

data.hint: Choose the correct reduced relative clause.
data.question: The proposals ___ at the meeting yesterday will be reviewed by the steering committee next week.

explanation.text: A reduced relative clause uses a past participle ('discussed') to replace a passive relative clause ('which were discussed'). The proposals did not discuss; they were discussed.
explanation.formula: Noun + past participle (replacing 'which/that + be + past participle')
examples: The book written by Hemingway is a classic.
The items sold at this store are handmade.

data.hint: Choose the correct discourse marker to indicate result.
data.question: The experiment yielded inconclusive results, ___ prompting the research team to redesign the methodology entirely.

explanation.text: 'Thereby' is an adverb meaning 'by that means' or 'as a result of that', and it is commonly followed by a present participle ('prompting') to show the consequence of the main clause.
explanation.formula: Main clause, + thereby + present participle
examples: He signed the contract, thereby agreeing to the terms.
The road was blocked, thereby forcing us to take a detour.

data.hint: Choose the correct word to form a formal conditional inversion.
data.question: ___ he succeed in his endeavors, he will have only his own relentless perseverance to thank.

explanation.text: 'Should' can be used at the beginning of a conditional clause to replace 'If', creating a formal and somewhat tentative condition (First Conditional inversion).
explanation.formula: Should + subject + base verb, + main clause
examples: Should you need any help, please call me.
Should it rain, the event will be moved indoors.

data.hint: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.

explanation.text: When 'regret' refers to feeling sorry about a past action, it is followed by a gerund ('telling'). 'Regret to tell/inform' is only used when announcing bad news in the present moment (e.g., 'I regret to inform you that you failed').
explanation.formula: regret + verb-ing (for past actions)
examples: I regret saying those harsh words.
She regrets quitting her job.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb forms for this mixed conditional sentence.
data.question: If he ___ a more cautious driver, he ___ that accident last night.

explanation.text: This is a mixed conditional. The 'if' clause describes a general, ongoing unreal present state (second conditional: 'were'), while the main clause describes a specific unreal past result (third conditional: 'wouldn't have had').
explanation.concept: Combining present unreal conditions with past unreal results
explanation.formula: If + subject + past simple, subject + would have + past participle
examples: If I were taller, I would have reached the top shelf.
If she spoke French, she would have gotten the job in Paris.
